name: Aloe leaf extract

lead: Aloe leaf extract is a staple of after-sun gels, moisturizers, sunscreens and facial products. People use it to soothe and hydrate skin so it looks calmer and smoother.

The clear inner gel is mostly water and contains the polysaccharide acemannan. Wikipedia describes the evidence for burns and wounds as conflicting, and small registered trials are mostly in oral and gum conditions. None in the sources reviewed test cosmetic appearance.

paras: Applied as a gel or in lotions, commonly after sun exposure or as a light daily moisturizer on irritated or dry skin.

Topical use in small amounts is likely safe, with allergic reactions possible. Oral latex or whole-leaf extract is linked to cramps, diarrhea and hepatitis, and regulators have acted on aloin laxatives; the cosmetic limit on anthraquinones is 50 ppm.

angle.text: Aloe gel soothes and hydrates skin, so it looks calmer and smoother after sun or irritation. Evidence on wound healing is conflicting, and its effect on appearance specifically is lightly studied.

lead: Aloe leaf extract is a preparation from the leaves of Aloe vera, a succulent plant long used on the skin, with records of use dating to the fourth millennium BCE [1]. In cosmetics it is a common soothing and moisturizing ingredient in lotions, gels, sunscreens, shampoos and facial products [1].

The leaf yields two main materials. The clear inner gel contains the polysaccharide acemannan, while the yellow latex contains aloin, an anthraquinone with laxative properties that is considered toxic [1]. The cosmetic industry limits anthraquinone content in aloe extracts to 50 parts per million [1].

Wikipedia describes the evidence for burns and wounds as conflicting, and says topical use in small amounts is likely safe with allergic reactions possible [1]. Laboratory studies report antibacterial and anti-tumor-promoting activity of aloe preparations [2][3], and several small trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov test aloe gel in oral and gum conditions [4][5].

paras: Aloe gel is added to lotions, soaps, moisturizers and makeup, and is traditionally applied to minor burns, abrasions, insect bites and windburn [1]. The gel is mildly acidic, with a pH of about 4.4 to 4.7, which can sting irritated skin [1]. Whole-leaf extracts and latex-containing products differ from decolorized gel in anthraquinone content, which is the basis of most safety regulation [1].

Aloe is a widespread after-sun and soothing ingredient and appears in simple routines for sensitive or irritated skin. In the sources reviewed there is no community discussion material to document, so claims about it are limited to those made by product marketers and the traditional uses above.

In a laboratory comparison, aloe vera gel extracts showed antibacterial activity against bacteria associated with skin infection, tested alongside antibiotics [2]. In a mouse model of chemically induced skin tumors, oral aloe leaf extract and topical aloe gel were reported to reduce the number and size of papillomas [3]. These are in-vitro and animal findings.

Topical use of small amounts is likely safe, and allergic reactions can occur [1]. Taking latex or whole-leaf extract by mouth has been associated with abdominal cramps, diarrhea and hepatitis, and chronic ingestion with other harms; aloe may interact with drugs including anticoagulants, diabetes medications and digoxin, and is advised against during pregnancy [1]. The US FDA banned aloin-based over-the-counter laxatives in 2002 after manufacturers did not provide adequate safety data, California lists non-decolorized whole-leaf extract as a chemical known to cause cancer, and the IARC has classified whole-leaf extract as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B) [1].

Registered trials in the sources reviewed test aloe gel mainly in oral and dental contexts: aloe vera against chlorhexidine for traumatic oral ulcers in 140 participants [4], and aloe vera gel compared with clindamycin gel as an addition to scaling and root planing for periodontitis [5]. Results are not summarized in the sources reviewed. Wikipedia reports that evidence for topical use in burns and wounds is conflicting, and that topical use may ease symptoms of psoriasis, acne and rashes [1]. No trial in the sources reviewed tests aloe leaf extract for cosmetic appearance outcomes.
